body:
## Module 4 in two minutes

**IBM consolidated HR service delivery and nobody used it. So they shut off the email address and the phone line**, and told around 21,000 managers their HR partners were no longer available for routine questions `[V]`.

**Service satisfaction fell to −35. They held.** The far side: ~94% of questions resolved without escalation, recovery to **+74**, and a **40% cut to the HR operating budget.** *(A correction that matters for this audience: −35 and +74 are an internal customer-satisfaction score for the HR service, not eNPS. The two get conflated everywhere.)*

**The trough is the shape of the curve, not evidence of failure.** Service genuinely gets worse until habit forms and edge cases are absorbed.

**So the binding constraint is not technology or design. It is sponsor tolerance.** Transformations die at month four, when the numbers are worst and somebody senior proposes a pause. **Pausing at the bottom guarantees the whole cost with none of the benefit**, and teaches the organization these things get abandoned when they get hard.

## The rule

**Set the tolerance in advance, in a number, and say it to the person who will ask you in month four.**

*"Satisfaction will fall. I expect around X before recovery. Below Y, or no turn by [date], we stop. Between those we hold, and I'm telling you now so I can point at this conversation later."*

A tolerance you haven't socialized isn't a tolerance. Most people set theirs too shallow, which is what −35 is for.

## What the full module adds

The case's honest limits. One organization, its own accounts, and the survivorship problem, since the functions that shut off the phone line and never recovered don't publish. **The sequencing rule**: no standing to tell another function to redesign until you have done it to your own, argued as practical rather than moral, because the question they will ask is what it actually costs, and only a practitioner can answer. That is also how Module 3's scope fight is won. **And the move that makes the cut credible rather than cold**: IBM raised entry-level hiring while cutting the budget, because automating junior work and cutting junior hiring dries the well in three to five years. Four transformations to judge, only one of which survives month six. And the activity: what you cut, **what it funds**, and what you protect.
